title: Crosswalk
intro: Crosswalk keeps changing the format in which a person can speak: warning, provocation, collective permission, official application, tourist welcome, payment alert, complaint and last words. Each format briefly supplies authority before the next punctures it. The money becomes game currency and the fearless troublemaker becomes someone apologising for inconvenience. Painted street markings bring the sequence back to a visible line and to Zebra's name. The song enjoys how easily language can manufacture a grand scene, while repeatedly exposing the flimsy material underneath.
reading: Rapid changes of speaking role; grand public promises fail at the point of material delivery.

revisions.33-phrase-line: He claims not to see a moral limit, and the verse immediately starts manufacturing visible lines in white paint. The abstraction becomes a crosswalk and then the zebra chant. That is a local sequence of language turning concrete, not just an isolated animal pun. It also suits a speaker whose deliberate provocation contradicts his claim to have no calculating angle: blindness is a performed excuse, rather than the absence of action.
revisions.editorial-33-reporting: A person who just declared freedom from law suddenly reports upward and formally applies for an appliance. The shift makes authority a role he can enter or leave by changing his diction. That matters more than assigning every passage to one stable speaker such as a specific official. The song is playing the formats themselves, letting a command, an application and a notification each momentarily organise the world.
revisions.editorial-33-needs: The promise to meet everyone's needs turns into a plan for a highly rated tourist attraction. Care for people and promotion of a place occupy the same reassuring register, although they are not the same achievement. The payment that follows then proves to be game money. Across the sequence, impressive language keeps offering value whose practical substance disappears when somebody tries to receive it.
revisions.editorial-33-final-apology: The heading 'last words' gives an ordinary apology an extreme setting. The person who began by dismissing consequences now imagines leaving behind inconvenience for the group. But the track then returns to the opening boast rather than ending at this confession. It cycles through a moment of social obligation and back into bravado, leaving neither the fearless persona nor the apologetic one as its sole identity.
